articles.title: Canelo Alvarez, a kingdom under attack and the price of boxing's biggest payday
articles.summary: As deadly attacks shake Saudi Arabia, Alvarez is pressing ahead with another enormous payday while other major sporting events in the region have been cancel...
articles.body:
In 1993, Wu-Tang Clan used the backronym C.R.E.A.M. (Cash Rules Everything Around Me) to explore the idea that we are all slaves to the dollar and that cash is king. Throughout the song, various members of the group took it in turns to rap about selling drugs or sticking up white boys on ball courts, anything to get by. It was, for all its swaggering energy, a cautionary tale; closer to a lamentation than a celebration.

In boxing, the same backronym is applicable. It can be applied not only in its original form, but will make just as much sense if you replace the word "Cash" with "Canelo." After all, in boxing, Saul "Canelo" Alvarez rules everything around us. He has for some time.

For proof of this, consider how the Mexican's WBC super middleweight title challenge against Christian Mbilli in Saudi Arabia on Saturday will proceed as planned despite the ongoing missile and drone attacks in Riyadh and the closing of King Khalid International Airport. Consider, too, if only for context, the fact that last Wednesday the U.S. State Department was concerned enough to order non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia following a series of deadly attacks by Houthi rebels, which have so far claimed the lives of at least 20 people and injured at least 370.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," said State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott. "The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them."

As expected, several major sporting events in Saudi Arabia have been canceled due to the recent attacks, including the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament, the Saudi International golf tournament, and even a world title fight on Alvarez's own card . However, the world championship boxing match between Alvarez (63-3-2, 39 KOs) and Mbilli (29-0-1, 24 KOs) has somehow stood firm and survived. Not only has Canelo made the trip to Riyadh, but Canelo, according to Turki Alalshikh at least, "fears nothing."

True or not, we can be sure of this much: Canelo, now 36 years of age, has not boxed since losing to Terence Crawford 13 months ago and would, in an ideal world, box again after this weekend as soon as February. The reason for that is quite simple. "I want to fight quick, like in February, because I have two fights left in Riyadh," he told The Ring . "So, I want to fight this one in Riyadh [against Mbilli], and then in February, the next one."

In other words, Canelo wants to get in and get out — as fast as he can. This pertains to Saturday night, when he challenges once more for the WBC super middleweight belt, and perhaps more generally, too. He is, after all, now on borrowed time. His conqueror, Terence Crawford, announced his own retirement at the end of last year and Alvarez, who turned professional at the age of 15, will be aware he has only so many big fights left. For now, he might be content to take the vast sums of money on offer in Saudi Arabia. But, beyond that, one would presume he has other plans. The kind of plans that bring him closer to home. The kind of plans that make him feel more comfortable and further enhance his legacy.

Until then, he will naturally go where the cash is, safe in the knowledge that everyone will follow. They will follow Canelo, irrespective of risk, because the sport ultimately revolves around him. More than that, the sport still needs him.

One man who has followed Canelo to Riyadh this week is Robert Diaz, the former longtime matchmaker for Golden Boy Promotions who has followed the Mexican great for some time. His wife, Karla, has worked for Alvarez for 15 years and therefore it was never a question that the couple would end up in Riyadh this weekend. Both knew it wouldn't be as easy getting there as it was when Alvarez fought William Scull in 2025 , of course, but that wasn't to say it couldn't be done.

"It was alright," Diaz told me last Friday. "I flew from LA to Rome, which was fine, and then Rome to Qassim Airport [in Buraidah, Saudi Arabia], but we couldn't take off because of luggage. There was a little delay, but it wasn't to do with the attacks or anything.

"Then, once we got in the air and landed, we had to go to Riyadh on the road for four hours. But we got here eventually and everything seems fine — so far."

Though keen to stress "so far," Diaz was just as keen to affirm his confidence in a situation like this one. "There's been no indication that it [the event] would get cancelled," he said. "You would think that would be a possibility, but when everything seemed to be moving forward, we were like, 'Are you sure?' And yeah, they were. They were buying travel and arranging everything, so at that point it was, 'OK.'

"It's funny because last year, after Canelo fought here [against Scull], I ended up going to Pakistan to do a WBA (World Boxing Association) event and they were at war with India. The airspace kept closing while I was there and there was a chance we weren't going to get out in time. In the end, though, we were fine. So, with this one, there was a sense of, 'Been there, done that. Let's go.'"

The thing is, they could have all been in Las Vegas, the fight capital of the world, this weekend. That is where fight fans typically gather in large numbers and where Canelo Alvarez is always welcome. It is there that, since the retirement of Floyd Mayweather, Canelo has become a headline attraction, often appearing at the T-Mobile Arena or MGM Grand on Cinco de Mayo and Mexican Independence Day.

In fact, the last time I saw Canelo in Las Vegas, he was there to complete his trilogy with Gennadiy Golovkin in 2022. It was September, the weekend of Mexican Independence, and for the Grand Arrivals at the MGM Grand the fighter was welcomed by the trumpets and violins of a mariachi band, as well as scores of screaming girls wearing bandanas. Then on Friday night, 24 hours before the fight, there was sudden gridlock along The Strip as countless heavy-duty vehicles sporting Mexican flags and relentlessly beeping horns crawled into town, windows down, heads out.

At one point, just to gauge the level of his popularity, I decided to visit the Grand and Co. shop in the MGM Grand lobby. That tends to be where fight merchandise is sold ahead of a big event and, for Canelo-Golovkin III, they were selling merch for both boxers, with one clearly outselling the other. "Canelo sells more by quite a distance and always outsells his opponents whenever he fights here," revealed Jodi, who ran the store and had been working there "too long to remember and long enough to remember them all [the great boxers]." She then shot me a look of horror when I had the nerve to propose Canelo's selling power might be comparable to Floyd Mayweather's. "Oh, come on," Jodi said. "Mayweather was much more popular. Him against [Manny] Pacquiao [in 2015]?" She rolled her eyes while making a whooshing sound with her mouth. "That was like nothing else. But, of course, they're both retired now and we miss them. Canelo is the next best thing."

While Mayweather remains the undisputed king of Las Vegas, Canelo did manage to do something in America that Mayweather never did: fight regularly in stadiums. This he did against Terence Crawford in his last fight (Vegas' new Allegiant Stadium), as well as in fights against Liam Smith and Billy Joe Saunders (AT&T Stadium in Texas), and Avni Yildirim (Hard Rock Stadium in Miami).

"Canelo was a stadium fighter," said Doug Fischer, the editor-in-chief at The Ring magazine. "They were huge fights and it didn't matter who the f*** he was fighting. You think the people in Texas knew who Liam Smith was? Liam put up a hell of a fight that night, it was entertaining, but they didn't know who the f*** he was.

"Stadium fights are rare in America. What I noticed that night [in Texas] was that one, Mexico definitely showed up, and two, there were entire families there. I was struck by the number of young females and older women: Moms, aunties. Somebody would be holding a baby or pushing a stroller. They all had the Canelo stuff on. They had the merch, the headbands. It reminded me of [Julio Cesar] Chavez, back when he was the man, the idol. I'm thinking, ' This must have been what it was like to be at a Julio Cesar Chavez fight back in the early nineties .' I don't think he [Alvarez] reached the heights of Chavez, but he got close — as close as anyone has since. I can't think of a Mexican fighter or American fighter who can reach those heights now. I just don't see it."

The key to seeing anything, I suppose, is visibility. In the case of Canelo, that means showcasing him on stages that are large, accessible, and safe. His next fight with Mbilli, for instance, could have quite easily found a home in a stadium, whether in the U.S. or elsewhere. It is arguably a better fight than some of those stadium fights previously mentioned and Mbilli is no less famous than some of those Canelo opponents in the eyes of the public. Besides, Canelo is someone who is by now accustomed to having the biggest stage and audience possible. Anything less would seem to undermine what got him here.

"Canelo had a couple of things going for him when he started more than 20 years ago," said Fischer. "One, he was able to stay active by modern standards. Also, being Mexican, he turned pro when he was 15 and he caught the eye of certain network executives. Because he had white skin and red hair, there was a network, Televisa, that started showcasing Canelo and the ratings were really good. They liked him. He was a humble kid. He looked like a boy but he was in there with men and he was fighting tooth and nail and showing a lot of heart. He had an entertaining style and most of the time he would get a knockout, too, which helps.

"I think probably by the time he was 16 years old he was moved up to main-event status because he was boosting their ratings. For a couple of years, from 16 to 18, he was headlining shows on network television the way boxing stars used to in America. 'Sugar' Ray Leonard out of the Olympics was doing the same thing. He would be fighting at seven o'clock or eight o'clock on ABC to a huge market share.

"That's how all these guys became household names. Someone like Ray 'Boom Boom' Mancini was a guy I grew up watching on regular TV on a Saturday afternoon, and Canelo got that same treatment in Mexico as a teenager. Before he had even set foot on American soil as an 18-year-old, he was a household name in Mexico. Because of that, and because of the large Mexican contingent in Southern California, if there's a buzz about an athlete in Mexico it's going to translate here. So, there was already curiosity about him. He already had a ready-made fan base. For his first fight in the U.S., at a casino out here [Morongo Casino Resort & Spa in Cabazon, California], there were fans that had made banners and stuff. Even before 'Canelo' had caught on as a nickname, these banners would say: 'Saul Alvarez.' There was already a group — a little cheering section — waiting for him."

With his heart set on becoming an international star, this early interest from the Mexican people didn't go unnoticed or unappreciated. It was in fact something Canelo and his team were eager to cultivate.

"To his credit, he wanted to be a star; he wanted to be that guy ," said Fischer. "When he would do a media workout, or a workout open to the public, he would spar. He did that for a long time. Only Mexican fighters ever did that. Nowadays fighters are so secretive. They feel self-conscious even working the mitts in public. But the Mexicans, around the time I started covering the sport, would be having sparring sessions and the fans would take the day off work to go watch.

"That kind of ended in the '90s, but Canelo brought it back and was doing this until maybe 2012 or 2013. I appreciated it. So did others. He got it: I've got to give the dudes something to make them become Canelo fans . He understood that.

"Today, fans are not high on the priority list. And if the fans aren't a priority, then the fans aren't going to prioritize these fighters. So, how do you build somebody into an attraction, to the level of Canelo, if you don't have that kind of connection or relationship?"

"Solitude is an Anglo-Saxon concept," wrote Lucia Berlin in her short story "Fool to Cry." "In Mexico City, if you're the only person on a bus and someone gets on they'll not only come next to you, they will lean against you."

Since beating Kermit Cintron in Mexico City in 2011, Canelo Alvarez has fought just once in his home country and that was against John Ryder, from Great Britain, in 2023. That, too, is somewhere he could have fought Christian Mbilli this weekend. He could have fought him in Mexico City, where he stopped Cintron in Round 5, or even in Guadalajara, where he was pushed hard for 12 rounds by Ryder and where Alvarez was born and raised.

"It's strange," said Ryder, the last man to box Canelo in Mexico. "I don't actually think Canelo is as popular as you think he is in Mexico. A lot of people see him as a bit of a 'sellout.' He has always been thinking about the legacy he wants to leave behind, but he probably needs to take a fight back to Mexico and win the fans back. I know the stadium was packed for our fight, but around the hotel and stuff, there wasn't a lot of interest in it. It wasn't like everybody was talking about Canelo or supporting him. I think they genuinely see him as a 'sellout.'"

Ryder, who is now retired, added: "He has been a remarkable sportsman for Mexico and what he has done in the sport has been amazing. But I think a lot of his fans wanted these big events — these career-defining fights — in Mexico and to feel like they were part of it. Most people in Mexico can't afford these big trips to the U.S. to watch him at the T-Mobile Arena or the MGM Grand. That will have hurt his legacy a bit in their eyes. It won't hurt his legacy in terms of who he has fought and what he has achieved, but when most of your big moments have happened in Vegas …

"Once he is back from Saudi, all he probably needs is a fight at the Azteca [Stadium in Mexico City] to finish off his career. Get 100,000 fans in there and that will be the cherry on the cake for him and his career."

Although currently in Riyadh taking one day at a time, Robert Diaz is still able to imagine and predict Alvarez's future. He, like Ryder, sees the importance of bringing the show back home and repaying those fans who once made banners and booked days off work to watch their hero spar.

"I think that is definitely a goal Canelo has," said Diaz. "There have been reports that he has talked to the owner of the Azteca Stadium, where Julio Cesar Chavez once fought [against Greg Haugen in 1993]. There have also been talks regarding his last fight being in Guadalajara, where he is from. So, I believe that is something that is on his mind. It would be huge for him to be able to go back and say, 'Thank you for all the love and support.'"

Fighting Canelo in Mexico was, according to Ryder, a "crazy experience," of which he has only fond memories. He might have lost the fight, but the acclaim he received from the Mexican fans, all of whom acknowledged his warrior spirit, felt almost as good as winning it. Indeed, whereas some of Canelo's previous opponents deemed victory the signing of the contract — that is, securing a career-high payday — Ryder viewed Canelo as more than just a cash cow. For the 12 rounds he spent in his company, he saw him as a beatable equal.

"I was a Canelo fan long before I was a rival of his," Ryder said. "It was kind of a pinch-me moment, but I had done the work not to show him too much respect or get too emotionally involved. The fight was just work time. It was the way it had to be. We were there to have a fight and that's how I wanted it to be. I didn't want to be all nicey-nicey with him. It was strictly business.

"On the night he wasn't as physically strong as I thought he would be. I was able to push him around a bit. If not for my nose 'going' in round two, I might have had even more success. But his accuracy was unbelievable, brilliant. When he throws a shot, he throws it with bad intentions and nine out of 10 times he lands it. His ring craft is great: his little double steps, how he feints, how he purposely telegraphs something and then throws something else. He is a special fighter."

Unlike world champions, who can be located on every street corner in boxing, special fighters are rare. Customarily, a special fighter is the kind of fighter who can bring tens of thousands of Mexicans to Las Vegas on Cinco de Mayo and Mexican Independence weekend; a special fighter is a fighter who can fill outdoor stadiums in countries not known for stadium fights; a special fighter is a fighter who can ensure a fight in a "warzone" somehow takes place.

A special fighter is also someone whose absence the sport tends to feel.

"One hundred percent we will miss him," said Ryder. "We never really replaced Mayweather, did we? Once Canelo goes, we need someone who can command those two big dates — in May and September — and deliver big fights every year. Canelo tried to fill that gap when Mayweather retired, but he still wasn't able to live up to the hype of Mayweather."

"We go through this process of missing fighters and mourning them with each generation," said Diaz. "We missed Julio [Cesar Chavez] when he was gone, we missed Oscar [De La Hoya] when he was gone, and we missed Floyd when he was gone. We will miss Canelo the same way. But there seems, at least historically, to always be that next guy who fills in. Hopefully we find it in a [Jaime] Munguia, or an [Rafael] Espinoza, who I am really high on. He also fights on Saturday's card [in Riyadh] and he is a kid with a lot of discipline and talent.

"Throughout history Mexico has always been very important to boxing and boxing has always been very important to Mexico. We have had a lot of world champions and idols from Mexico, but we haven't always had a lot of big global stars. Now, because the focus is no longer on creating these heroes and these idols, I think Canelo is that last Mohican; the last guy capable of drawing thousands of people over to the big events. He has maybe two or three fights left and we need to appreciate that. It always happens: once they are gone, even the haters start missing them. We will soon miss the kind of nights Canelo has given us."

This Saturday, on shaky ground, Saul "Canelo" Alvarez will give us another one of those nights, albeit slightly different from the usual. After that, at some point in 2027, he will get on a bus in Mexico City, sit beside someone who speaks his language, and lean against them in order to rest his heavy head on their shoulder. " Bienvenido a casa," he will then hear them say. "Te extrañamos."

Or in English: "Welcome home. We have missed you."

Elliot Worsell is a boxing writer whose byline first appeared in Boxing News magazine at the age of 17. He has, in the 20 years since, written for various publications, worked as press officer for two world heavyweight champions, and won four first-place BWAA (Boxing Writers Association of America) awards. In addition to his boxing writing, Worsell has written about mixed martial arts for Fighters Only magazine and UFC.com. He has also written two non-fiction books, one of which, Dog Rounds, was shortlisted at the British Sports Book Awards in 2018. He lives in London, England and his writing can currently be found at Uncrowned.com and Boxingscene.com.

articles.title: Father's death, thoughts of quitting wrestling, a promise and World Championship gold: Manisha Bhanwala's story
articles.summary: The first thing Manisha Bhanwala wanted to show the world after becoming a world champion was not her medal.
articles.body: The first thing Manisha Bhanwala wanted to show the world after becoming a world champion was not her medal. It was a white T-shirt carrying photographs of her parents.As the 29-year-old wrestler celebrated her historic World Championships gold, she held up the T-shirt for everyone to see. There were no words needed to explain the moment. It was her way of bringing her parents into a success they had always dreamed of but her father did not live to witness.Manisha defeated American Abigail Nette 8-6 in a thrilling comeback victory in the final to become the first Indian woman wrestler to win a World Championships gold. But behind this historic achievement was a personal story of loss, family sacrifices and a promise she had made to herself.Her father, Suresh, passed away in 2022. Four years later, Manisha has fulfilled the dream he had for his daughter.The day that changed Manisha's lifeManisha's journey in wrestling began with inspiration from her own family. Growing up in a farming family in Jind, Haryana, she watched her elder brother Rinku play kabaddi in the village. That was what first made her interested in sports.With several members of the family involved in sports, taking up wrestling became a natural choice. Her brother plays kabaddi, while her sister-in-law Mamta Sihag is also a wrestler.Rinku remembers that Manisha always had the physical strength and mental toughness needed to compete."We all played sports in the family. She used to watch me play kabaddi in the village and that inspired her. We then decided that she should take up an individual sport rather than a team game. She was physically strong and mental toughness was always her biggest strength," Rinku told PTI.However, one morning in 2022 brought a major setback in her life.Manisha was preparing to travel to Mongolia for the Asian Championships when tragedy struck. Her father had attended a 'jagran' the previous night. The following morning, he passed away in his sleep due to a cardiac arrest.The news left Manisha devastated. She was deeply attached to her family and could not imagine leaving home at such a difficult time. She even considered walking away from wrestling.Brother's words gave her the strength to continueThe family knew how much Manisha's father had sacrificed to help her become a wrestler. They did not want all those efforts to go in vain.Rinku and the other family members tried to convince her to continue with the tournament, reminding her of the dream their father had for her."She was preparing to leave, but our father passed away that very morning. He had attended a jagran and died in his sleep. She was so attached to all of us that she did not want to go."We had to tell her that all the efforts our father had made to make her a wrestling champion would go to waste if she gave up. We somehow convinced her to board the flight to Mongolia," Rinku recalled.Manisha eventually travelled to Mongolia and returned with a bronze medal from the Asian Championships.That was an important moment in her career. She continued competing and went on to win three more Asian medals, including a gold last year.But the biggest prize was still waiting for her.She carried her parents to the World ChampionshipsBefore leaving for Astana for the World Championships, Manisha decided to do something special. She got photographs of her parents printed on a white T-shirt.It was not just something she wanted to wear during the competition. She had a clear purpose behind it. She wanted to win the gold medal and show the T-shirt to the world.Her brother said she was determined to make that moment happen."She had got the pictures of our parents printed on a white T-shirt before leaving for Astana. It was her determination that she would win gold and show that T-shirt to everyone. She did exactly that," Rinku said.And she kept her promise.After fighting back to beat Abigail Nette 8-6 in the final, Manisha displayed the T-shirt. The celebration was about more than becoming a world champion. It was about a father who had believed in her and a family that had stood by her through difficult times.Rinku said the victory had fulfilled a dream shared by the entire family."It was our family's dream that she become a world champion, and today she has achieved it. This is even more special for our father. His dream and the dream of the entire family have come true," he added.A long journey across weight categoriesManisha's road to the top was also marked by several changes in weight categories. She competed in the 62kg, 65kg and 57kg divisions before finding her biggest success in the non-Olympic 59kg category.At 29, she has finally reached the top of world wrestling.Her journey began in a village in Haryana, where watching her brother play kabaddi introduced her to sports. It took her through personal tragedy, difficult decisions and years of hard work before she achieved what her father had always wanted.The gold medal belongs to Manisha. But the moment she held up that white T-shirt, she made sure her father's dream shared the spotlight.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Paddy Pimblett preferiría una revancha con Gaethje... a pelear contra Ilia Topuria
articles.summary: Aunque reconoce su "odio" hacia 'El Matador'
articles.body: El futuro de Paddy Pimblett (24-4) está por escribir. Tras la espectacular finalización vía sumisión el pasado mes de julio, antes de finalizar el primer minuto de combate, sobre Benoit Saint-Denis (17-4)... el de Liverpool sopesa sus próximos pasos en UFC. Y sobre la mesa, él mismo pone una revancha por el título contra Justin Gaethje (29-5). “Preferiría una revancha con Gaethje antes que pelear con Ilia Topuria, porque quiero ser campeón mundial”, declaraba el de Liverpool en una entrevista con 'How U Livin J Piven'. Algo que, no obstante, parece lejano... pues Tsarukyan (24-3) o el propio Topuria (17-1) están en la fila antes que el inglés, esperando. “Odio a Ilia, que quede claro… Obviamente, preferiría vencer a Ilia antes que a Justin, pero Justin tiene el cinturón y para eso peleamos. Para ser reconocidos como los mejores del mundo, para ser el campeón indiscutible. Ese ha sido mi objetivo desde que tenía 15 o 16 años, así que eso es lo que quiero lograr”, añadía. Paddy, sin embargo, perdió ante Gaethje el pasado mes de enero en un combate celebrado por el título interino del peso ligero. Por lo tanto, parece que necesitaría, al menos, otro triunfo para volver a ser el contendiente número uno en la división de los 70 kilos. Lo que no está claro es si el campeón seguirá siendo Justin. “No creo que vuelva a pelear. Creo que sí, pero al mismo tiempo, no lo sé, porque nunca superará la euforia de ganar el cinturón en la Casa Blanca. Como me dijeron mis entrenadores: ‘Si estuvieras en esa situación, te diría que te retiraras’. No tiene sentido perseguir otra cosa cuando nunca volverá a sentir algo mejor que ganar ese cinturón en la Casa Blanca”, remataba el de Liverpool.

articles.title: Jean Silva pone a José Aldo por delante de Volkanovski en la 'pelea' por ser el GOAT del peso pluma
articles.standfirst: El peleador brasileño considera que su compatriota hizo más en la división de peso pluma que el australiano
articles.summary: El peleador brasileño considera que su compatriota hizo más en la división de peso pluma que el australiano
articles.body: Con su victoria en el pasado UFC 333 ante Movsar Evloev, Alexander Volkanovski se consagró para la mayoría como el GOAT de peso pluma. De hecho, este triunfo le permitió batir el récord de victorias en peleas por el cinturón de José Aldo, e incluso antes de lograrlo muchos ya le consideraban el mejor peleador de la historia de la categoría. Sin embargo, Jean Silva ha afirmado que su compatriota sigue por delante del australiano en el ránking histórico. Es cierto que Aldo fue pionero en la división, y que hasta el K.O. sufrido ante Conor McGregor en 13 segundos había barrido con toda la categoría. Sin embargo, su final de carrera fue muy diferente a cómo está siendo el de Volkanovski, aunque a Silva no le parezca suficiente para colocar a 'The Great' por delante del 'Rey de Río'. "Estamos hablando de diez años invicto y como campeón. Eso tiene mucho peso, y creo que Volk estaría de acuerdo. Si hay alguien con la experiencia y autoridad necesaria para hablar de esto, ese es el propio Volkanovski, y creo que él lo diría", afirmó 'Lord' en una entrevista con Ariel Helwani. Lo cierto es que el australiano siempre dice que no debe ser él el que le otorgue el título de GOAT, pero los números están ahí y sin duda son mejores que los de Aldo. Esto también se podría entender como una estrategia de Silva para provocar a Volkanovski y evitar que suba a peso ligero, ya que el peleador australiano ha reconocido que su plan es volver a intentar ser doble campeón antes de retirarse de una vez por todas. Obviamente, Jean quiere medirse a 'The Great' por el cinturón antes de que eso suceda, y no es la primera vez que intenta que el australiano pique el anzuelo. "Resulta desconcertante ver que este tipo, que lleva mucho tiempo en esto, piense que, al observar aquellos momentos contra Diego Lopes, yo me convertiría en un blanco fácil en el suelo", reconoció Silva en la misma entrevista. Aún así, en su última pelea finalizó a José Delgado, que ni siquiera forma parte del top 15 de la categoría, por lo que todavía tiene que remar para ganarse esa oportunidad. De hecho, estas palabras vienen por las declaraciones de Joe López -entrenador de Volkanovski- en una entrevista con 'Submission Radio', donde dijo que "no creo que se haya ganado su lugar. Hay muchos otros por delante de él que han tenido un desempeño mucho mejor, como Aljamain Sterling. Es un tipo con mucha fuerza, y eso es todo lo que tiene. Si te alcanza con uno de sus golpes, obviamente puede noquearte; pero, viendo cómo Diego lo dominó en el suelo —prácticamente lo destrozó—, si Alex lograra llevarlo al suelo, todo habría terminado. No hay duda al respecto". El beef está servido.

articles.title: Canelo vs. Mbilli weigh-in results: Canelo Alvarez comes in lighter than WBC champ for comeback bout
articles.summary: Saul "Canelo" Alvarez has cleared his final hurdle before Saturday's comeback bout against WBC super middleweight champion Christian Mbilli.
articles.body:
Saul "Canelo" Alvarez has cleared his final hurdle before Saturday's comeback bout against WBC super middleweight champion Christian Mbilli .

Alvarez and Mbilli both met their required weights Friday in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, rendering their championship bout official. Alvarez, amid the revelry of mariachi music and WBO featherweight champion Rafael Espinoza belting out tunes on the microphone, came in slightly lighter at 167.6 pounds, while the heavily muscled Cameroonian-Frenchman tipped the scales at a 167.8 pounds.

Afterward, the two faced off in their final staredown before Saturday's title bout .

"This is very important for me," Alvarez said through a translator. "I've been doing this for the last 21 years. I won my first title 16 years ago, so it's very important for me to be here, to take that title, and obviously get back into that world championship corner.

"He's never faced anybody like that, so tomorrow I'm going to teach him exactly what it is to face somebody like me."

Saturday's fight marks Alvarez's first appearance in more than 13 months, following his unanimous decision loss to Terence Crawford in September 2025 . Alvarez (63-3-2, 39 KOs), 36, subsequently underwent surgery on his left elbow and spent much of the past year recovering. The Mexican superstar now has an opportunity to reclaim one of the super middleweight titles he lost to Crawford, who retired from boxing in December.

Standing in his way is Mbilli (29-0-1, 24 KOs), the undefeated 31-year-old who was elevated to full WBC super middleweight champion following Crawford's retirement. Mbilli last competed on the same September 2025 card as Alvarez, fighting Lester Martinez to a split draw. Saturday represents the biggest fight of Mbilli's career and his first defense of the WBC championship.

"Tomorrow night I'm going to beat him everywhere. Best conditioning, best punch, best technique. I'm going to put my 100% on my fight," Mbilli said.

"[This will be] the fight of the decade. It's the fight of the year, it will be an amazing fight. Don't miss this, it will be incredible."

The matchup headlines the "Mexico vs. The World" boxing event in Riyadh, which has drawn immense scrutiny for remaining in Saudi Arabia despite escalating regional conflicts and missile and drone attacks that have disrupted international travel and forced the postponement or cancellation of other major sporting events.

Saturday's card also features WBA super middleweight champion Jaime Munguia (167.4) taking on Nikita Zon (167.5) in the co-feature, while Rafael Espinoza (125.8) is scheduled to defend his WBO featherweight championship against Ricardo Blandon (126).

articles.title: Mbili vs Alvarez: Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez makes weight against backdrop of Saudi turmoil
articles.summary: Christian Mbilli and Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez make weight for their world title bout in Riyadh just 24 hours after two ballistic missiles are intercepted over the Saudi Arabian capital.
articles.body:
Christian Mbilli and Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez made weight for their world title bout in Riyadh just 24 hours after two ballistic missiles were intercepted over the Saudi Arabian capital.

Mbilli, 31, was elevated to WBC super-middleweight champion in January and makes his first defence against Mexico's Alvarez, 36, on Saturday.

Both fighters tipped the scales at 12st (76kg) before engaging in a tense but respectful face-off.

Alvarez, who will step into the ring for the 69th time on Saturday, made his professional debut almost exactly 21 years ago on 29 October 2005.

"This is very important for me, I've been doing this for 21 years and won my first world title 16 years ago. It's important for me to win a title again," Alvarez said.

"My experience is different, he hasn't faced anyone like me and I'll teach him tomorrow."

Doubts have been raised in recent weeks about whether the event can take place safely due to the growing conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement.

The UK's Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) currently advises against all but essential travel to the whole of Saudi Arabia.

On Thursday, Saudi Press Agency reported the Civil Defence had intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh. A civilian sustained a minor injury and there was damage to a house and vehicle due to falling shrapnel.

Earlier in October, a missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 .

Travel arrangements for those attending Saturday's bout have been complicated by restricted access to the airport.

While other sporting events in Saudi Arabia - including The Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition , the final round of the 2026 World Rally Championship and the 2026 Urban Cycling World Championships - have been cancelled the combat sports world has not followed suit.

Friday's weigh-in began with a performance from a Mariachi band, with the card billed as Mexico v the world.

Four-weight world champion Alvarez is fighting for the first time since losing to Terence Crawford in September 2025.

Saturday will be the first time Alvarez has entered a bout without a world title to his name since 2015.

Cameroon-born Mbilli, who trains in Canada, is yet to lose in 30 fights as a professional, winning 29 and drawing one, with 24 of those victories coming by stoppage.

"Tomorrow night I will beat him in every way. I have the best condition and technique," Mbilli said.

"A win would change my life a lot. It will be a fight of the year."

Meanwhile, Mexico's Jaime Munguia defends the WBA super-middleweight title against Nikita Zon in the co-main, and compatriot Rafael Espinoza puts his WBO featherweight belt on the line against Ricardo Blandon.

But Mexican Lindolfo Delgado withdrew from his bout against Russian-Canadian Artur Biyarslanov for the vacant IBF light-welterweight title earlier this week.

articles.title: Islam Makhachev Updates UFC Retirement Timeline Ahead of Prates-Morales Interim Title Fight
articles.summary: Islam Makhachev is apparently eyeing UFC retirement in the near future after delaying his defense of his UFC welterweight championship.
articles.body:
Islam Makhachev is apparently eyeing UFC retirement in the near future after delaying his defense of his UFC welterweight championship.

Makhachev, who was intended to fight at UFC 336 before an interim welterweight title bout between Carlos Prates and Michael Morales was scheduled instead, said in a Friday social media post his next fight will be "one of the last in my career."

"They say Prates is too dangerous for me and Morales is too good for me," Makhachev wrote. "So I want to face the best of them and prove to the world once again who is the best in world."

The UFC announced last week Prates would be taking on Morales for the interim belt this January rather than competing for a full championship against Makhachev.

UFC president and CEO Dana White said Makhachev was initially slated for the event at UFC 336 in Toronto, but Makhachev didn't want to fight until after Ramadan ends in early March, per CBS Sports' Brandon Wise .

Prates has since criticized Makhachev's decision in multiple social media posts, including one in which he told manager Ali Abdelaziz he planned to "finish [Makhachev's legacy]" when they eventually fought.

Makhachev competed in his lone fight of the year in August, when he defended his belt against Ian Machado Garry at UFC 330 in Philadelphia. He complained prior to the bout Morales was one of too many contenders waiting to challenge him for the welterweight title.

He will now be expected to face either Morales or Prates whenever the UFC can finalize his next title defense sometime in mid-2027.

articles.title: UFC: Islam Makhachev confirms retirement plans before Prates-Morales fight
articles.summary: UFC welterweight champion Islam Makhachev says his next fight will be "one of the last" of his illustrious career.
articles.body:
UFC welterweight champion Islam Makhachev says his next fight will be "one of the last" of his illustrious career.

The 35-year-old Russian beat Ian Machado Garry in August to defend his welterweight title in a 17th-straight victory in the UFC.

The win meant Makhachev, who is a former lightweight world champion, broke Anderson Silva's 13-year record for the longest win streak in UFC history.

Makhachev says he wants to prove again he is "the best in the world" by facing the winner of Brazil's Carlos Prates and Ecuador's Michael Morales.

The pair are set to fight for the interim welterweight belt at UFC 336 on 30 January.

"My next fight is one of the last in my career," said Makhachev.

"They say Prates is too dangerous for me and Morales is too good for me.

"So I want to face the best of them and prove to the world once again who is the best in world."

UFC president Dana White has said Makhachev was originally scheduled to defend his belt against Prates in January, but opted to delay fighting until after Ramadan in March.

White added he thought Makhachev was "holding up the division", which was why he chose to create the interim bout between Prates and Morales.

Makhachev later said the bout between the pair will determine "the true worthy contender".

Makhachev is widely regarded as one of the best fighters in UFC history after winning 29 of his 30 fights.

In August, White said Makhachev was "on the right path" to being regarded as the greatest fighter in the promotion's history.

Prates, 33, has won his last three fights by knockout, while Morales, 27, has won all 19 of his professional fights.

When Crawford retired it left the four major world championships vacant and Mbilli became the WBC titlist.

"I'm the challenger now, but in my mind I've always been the champion, ever since I was a little kid," Canelo said.

He elected to go straight in with Mbilli, a high-calibre, tough, aggressive fighter, right off the back of that defeat.

"I don't believe in shortcuts. I want to become a world champion again, and that's why I want to face the best. Mbilli is the world champion," Canelo said.

Mbilli, unbeaten with only one draw in his 30-fight professional career, declared: "I have a lot of respect for Canelo and his career, and I congratulate him on everything he has achieved. But inside the ring, it will be a different story, and I'm coming to win.

The event in Riyadh is going ahead amid escalating conflict in the region.

Houthi attacks have targeted Saudi airports, including Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, while security concerns have led to the postponement or cancellation of other sporting events in the kingdom.

"You know, fighting in Saudi for me is special and whatever it takes I'm going to be a world champion again," Canelo has said.

"Because I'm a fighter and I want to achieve a lot of things in boxing yet and that motivates myself. I love boxing."

Matthew Hatton boxed Canelo back in 2011, in the first world title fight of the Mexican superstar's career. He thinks this fight could affect Canelo's legacy.

"I do think he's still got enough left to beat Mbilli. I think it's an interesting fight," Hatton told the Toe2Toe podcast.

But he warned: "I know people say it doesn't tarnish their legacy but for me, slightly, it does. Say he was to lose to Mbilli on the weekend for me it does tarnish that a little bit.

"We all look at that differently. I would like to see him retire now.

"Personally I would like to see Canelo stop now, he's had such a good career, he's had a fantastic legacy and I think it's a shame when they go on too long."

articles.summary: El sevillano está a un paso del título en Cage Warriors
articles.body: El próximo 7 de noviembre, en los antiguos estudios de la BBC en Londres, Manuel del Valle ‘Mouzid’ (8-1) liderará el histórico ‘Spanish Showcase’ de Cage Warriors. El sevilla, convertido en una de las estrellas de la histórica promotora británica, está a un paso del título del peso wélter… y todo pasa por un triunfo ante Luan Darte (15-13) la próxima semana. Antes, desde Liverpool, atiende a MARCA. Pregunta. Se encuentra desde hace semanas en el Next Gen MMA de Liverpool, el gimnasio de Paddy Pimblett, Luke Riley, George Staines… ¿Qué tal por allí? Respuesta. La verdad es que me siento de lujo. Hoy justo hemos empezado la Fight Week, ya empieza lo duro, pero vamos, que se disfrute de la misma manera. Y ya está todo el trabajo hecho, falta la última parte. He estado prácticamente cuatro semanas aquí, en Liverpool, y la verdad es que el campamento es inmejorable. O sea, rodeado de un ambiente de primer nivel, de luchadores de UFC, de Oktagon, de PFL, compañeros de Cage Warriors… Entonces, al final, uno siente cada entrenamiento y cada semana que va pasando, el nivel de evolución que tiene aquí, cómo va afinando las cosas… La verdad es que me siento súper bien, súper preparado. Y, no sé, entrenar aquí, me está dando una confianza y una seguridad de que el trabajo lo he hecho lo mejor posible. Al final, no me pierdo prácticamente ninguna sesión y como lo único que hago aquí, en Liverpool, es entrenar, el tiempo libre lo dedico a estar con los compañeros, que me enseñen algún truco… P. Usted viene de un gimnasio modesto de Sevilla, el Sevilla Fight Center, que está haciendo las cosas bien. En España hay ejemplos de sitios que lo están haciendo muy bien… pero entiendo que cada vez que sale a Liverpool nota ese ‘salto’. R. En España, para mi opinión, el deporte está muy verde. Comparándolo con estos gimnasios así, que tienen un equipo profesional tan desarrollado, tan grande, y con gente en ligas tan grandes, creo que no hay ningún equipo así en España a día de hoy. Hay equipos ya que pueden tener pequeños grupos profesionales, como puede ser el caso del Climent o el Black Panther, también el Barcelona MMA Team… pero aquí al final tienen un sistema comprobado y es que llevan 15 años sacando gente a primer nivel, sacando gente que rinde y saca resultados en grandes ligas. Es algo que todavía en España creo que estamos en desarrollo y a mí la verdad es que me viene muy bien. Me han abierto las puertas, me han acogido muy bien y de momento en la etapa que estoy de mi carrera y espero que sea así durante mucho tiempo, es un sitio del que quiero seguir formando parte en cierta manera. P. Para que la gente más ajena al deporte lo entienda… ¿Cómo llega un peleador a poder formar parte de otro gimnasio durante, como es su caso, cuatro semanas? R. Yo he podido entrar y estoy entrando con el equipo profesional y demás por mi manager. Él tiene buena relación con el Next Gen. Yo le estuve preguntando por un gimnasio de Inglaterra que me recomendara para hacer el campamento. Él me dijo varios pero por mi perfil me recomendó el Next Gen. Me puso en contacto y me dijo que podría venirme mejor. Yo llegué como quien dice con una carta de recomendación y la manera en la que me han acogido también ha sido un poco distinta. Pero a partir de ahí, me han dicho muchas veces eso de que ‘eres un chaval normal’, que les he caído de puta madre y que soy como uno de ellos. P. Puede llegar usted con carta de recomendación pero luego el respeto hay que ganárselo… R. Claro. Después uno tiene que cumplir, uno tiene que rendir en los entrenamientos, ser buen compañero y dar la cara. Si ven que de verdad el tío viene a entrenar, que lo quiere es mejorar, que está continuamente intentando pasar el máximo tiempo posible en el gimnasio y todo… yo creo que a ellos les gusta. P. ¿Cambia su esquina para este combate? R. De momento sigo con Sevilla. O sea, de momento sigo 100% con Sevilla. De cara a futuro, no sé qué acabará pasando, la verdad que yo cada vez me encuentro más cómodo aquí. Y... te lo cuento como anécdota, ¿sabes?. En plan, esta vez, estos días, ellos mismos desde Liverpool me dijeron que si tenía esquina o necesitaba algo. Y más o menos me dejaron caer que yo puedo seguir. Yo al final si quiero estar contado con ellos, tendré que pasar aquí mucho más tiempo cada año. Con mi equipo, hasta el momento, me han ido las cosas muy bien y quiero seguir contando con ellos hasta el fin del mundo. La verdad que yo todo lo que sé es gracias a mi entrenador Iván, que es como mi segundo padre. Al final, aquí en Liverpool me siento en muchos aspectos como en casa y me están acogiendo muy bien, ¿sabes?. Para mi pelea me dan consejos, están perdiendo su tiempo teniendo aquí siete o ocho tíos que también van a pelear en breve… P. Ya está con un 6-1 en Cage Warriors. Wow. R. Sí… pero no es algo a lo que preste tanta atención. Yo al final me limito a hacer mi trabajo dentro de la jaula y dentro del gimnasio. Ya después esas cosas son del mánager, de la gente del mundillo y demás. Yo tengo que seguir cosechando buenos resultados, seguir rindiendo, y seguir dando la cara y demostrando que soy un prospecto ya no solo a nivel nacional, sino a nivel europeo, que soy uno de los nombres a tener en cuenta en la división. P. Pero se ha convertido en una cara muy reconocible dentro de Cage Warriors. Usted es el principal culpable de que Cage Warriors esté más cerca que nunca de las MMA españolas. Eso es innegable. R. Yo a lo mejor he sido el detonante, por así decirlo. Pero al final, el momento en el que estaban las MMA nacionales a nivel europeo… tanto por Ilia como por Joel, por Dani, por Hecher... o sea, después también las compañías españolas que están empezando a aparecer como WOW, AFL… Al final yo creo que ha sido un conjunto de todos, ¿sabes?. Y que yo al final he llegado aquí, gracias a Dios, y se están dando las cosas como se tienen que dar, estamos ganando las peleas, finalizándolas… y también cuando me ponen una cámara delante me desenvuelvo bien, con ese ‘spanglish’ mío. Y a los ingleses les gusta. Entonces ha sido como un cúmulo de cosas que han hecho que vean un mercado por explotar en España. También al final los periodistas en cierta manera también me han ayudado, bien dando la visibilidad que me han dado en España. Cage Warriors, por ejemplo, con vosotros, viendo todos los post colaborativos que tengo con MARCA… habrán dicho, ‘hostia, MARCA, que es un superperiódico en España, le está dando visibilidad a este chaval. En España este deporte es más grande de lo que pensamos’. Yo creo que como he dicho, ha sido un cúmulo de todo. Yo he podido ser el detonante, he podido ser la cara visible, pero ha sido un trabajo de mucha gente. P. Parece que lo de venir a España por parte de Cage Warriors se ha parado un poco… pero al menos han preparado este histórico evento en Londres como compensación. R. Vamos, prácticamente estaba todo cerrado para venir este año. Querían venir además en noviembre, en la fecha de este evento en Londres. El problema ha sido que se les ha echado un poco el tiempo encima, porque las ciudades que barajaban y eso son ciudades que al final tienen mucho volumen de ocio. Entonces, los sitios que valoraban, los estadios que ellos buscaban y demás… no estaban disponibles. Entonces querían hacerlo bien. Y para 2027, su idea es venir. Sobre todo en el primer semestre del año quieren cuadrar un evento. El año que viene, uno o dos eventos quieren hacer, es lo que me comentaron a mí. P. ¿Cómo ha notado usted la evolución del trato que le da Cage Warriors? Se ha convertido en una de las caras más visibles de la promotora. R. Pues, ya sabes, los andaluces somos gente muy cercana, entonces nosotros desde el minuto uno, tanto yo como mi equipo, que hemos llegado aquí con respecto a educación y todo, pues hemos creado un vínculo con todo el mundo… y he caído en gracia. Después han llegado los buenos resultados y encima ellos han puesto la vista sobre el mercado español. Ha sido un cúmulo de cosas y ellos han dicho ‘vamos a darle a este chaval visibilidad’. P. Siempre me ha dicho, a lo largo de las entrevistas que hemos tenido, que sus primeros recuerdos de MMA son ver combates de Cage Warriors, el recuerdo de las guantillas amarillas. Todavía no va a pelear por el cinturón pero se viene su primer Main Event. Es mucho decir. R. Sí, y ahora estos días estoy empezando a sacarle más valor. Han venido de CW al gimnasio a grabar y me veo más como cara del evento. Al final, para mí, ya solo estar aquí era un sueño. Y como tú has dicho antes, que ya sea una de las caras de la compañía, en cierta manera… pues todos los que han sido caras de la compañía en algún momento han destacado y han llegado a conseguir grandes cosas dentro del deporte. Si esta gente, que llevan casi 30 años en el deporte, están poniendo los ojos en mí, es que habrán visto algo. Y hay que empezar a darle valor, a creérselo un poquito más en ese aspecto y demás. P. Ha costado mucho encontrarle rival para este combate… R. Sí, la semana pasada creo que fue. Se valoraban otras cosas, se valoraba una pelea por cinturón… lo que pasa que es que los que podían pelear por cinturón o tenían peleas cerradas, o por tiempo… pues querían más tiempo para el campamento, que es algo totalmente respetable y demás. Me dijeron que si quería esperar pero me ofrecieron también ser este Main Event… y yo dije que vale. Yo quiero pelear. Pero al final se queda uno con el hecho de que, hostia, podría haber sido ya el cinturón… pero bueno, a mí me gusta mantenerme activo, seguir cosechando victorias. Ya no hay solo que pensar en ser campeón de Cage Warriors, sino ya lo que puede venir después. Y cosechar buenos resultados, al final, para otras promotoras y demás, es algo importante. P. A mucha gente le ha sorprendido que su rival sea un 15-13 como es Luan Duarte. Esperaban, quizás, otro récord… pero también hay que poner en valor a un luchador con casi 30 peleas profesionales y más triunfos que derrotas. R. Yo quería pelear, o sea, yo tampoco me fijo tanto en el récord. Yo me fijo en los recursos que tiene. Y si te fijas, sí, tendrá 13 derrotas, pero que llevan sin finalizar ocho años. Y en 13 derrotas lo han finalizado solo dos veces. Y tiene 15 victorias. Y muchas de ellas son finalizaciones. O sea, que es un tío que al final tiene peligro y demás. Yo he visto peleas suyas y es un tío que no entrega nunca la cuchara. Es un tío que está siempre intentando luchar, con los recursos que tiene y demás. Es un tío que le pesan las manos, tiene poder, que en sus últimas peleas se ha visto progresión. Para mí, en sus dos últimas peleas, tiene una victoria y una derrota. Y para mí, las dos últimas las gana, la anterior sí que la pierde, que es en Cage Warriors. Y el primer asalto lo gana. Es un tío que empieza fuerte los primeros asaltos. Que no es un tío que el récord puede engañar, pero que es un tío que tiene tablas. Al final son, como tú has dicho, casi 30 peleas profesionales, muchas finalizaciones, victorias en ligas importantes como Oktagon, victorias aquí en Europa, en ligas de Serbia y demás, experiencia en Cage Warriors… O sea que no es un tío que se pueda coger y decir que va a llegar y va a salir a cobrar... Yo tengo claro que va a buscar guerra y que quiere sumar una victoria. P. ¿Qué le falta a Mouzid para pelear por el título de Cage Warriors? R. Ya la idea era que estuviera peleando por el título. Lo que pasa es que no se han dado las circunstancias. O sea, yo espero que la próxima pelea ya sea por el cinturón. Si vuelve a pasar cualquier inconveniente o lo que sea, al final me limito a pelear… A mí lo que me gusta es pelear. Si no se da, es por algo. Todo en esta vida pasa por algo. Al final, sacando lo positivo de la situación, soy el Main Event de un evento que van a hacer en Londres para los españoles. Es que es algo histórico, es algo que hasta la fecha no había pasado. Es algo que ya se va a quedar para mí para el resto de mi vida. Eso es algo que hay que valorar. P. Entonces, siendo positivos, peleará por el cinturón el año que viene… R. Sí. La verdad que este año quiero pasar el Ramadán con familia. Y luego poder pelear a mediados o finales de abril. Por ahí. Pelear por el título sobre esas fechas me gustaría. Ahora en enero creo que me voy a ir a Tailandia, estar un mes entrenando por allí como el año pasado. Y luego a entrenar en Sevilla. Después del Ramadán, venir a Liverpool y preparar ese combate por el título. P. En recientes entrevistas ya ha empezado a hablar de UFC, Contender Series… ha cambiado un poco eso en usted, ¿no?. Antes solamente mencionaba Cage Warriors. Ya ve la meta más cerca, entiendo. R. Sí, lo veo más cercano. También tras la última victoria, el manager me lo comentó. Me dijo que si quería un Contender, que sin problema… Y yo le contesté que ya veía el cinturón cerca y que lo quería, que había dado mucho por saco con conseguirlo. También, no a través de mi manager, sino a través de otro lado, me han ofrecido ya varios cortos avisos para UFC y demás. Pero como yo digo, ya el siguiente paso natural, si seguimos cosechando victorias, buenos resultados y todo como estamos… Pero me gustaría ganar el cinturón de Cage Warriors y me gustaría defenderlo, porque yo soy de los que dice que uno no es campeón hasta que defiende su cinturón. Y ya luego pues me gustaría dar el paso a UFC, que al final, económicamente y en muchos aspectos, es algo que te ayuda mucho en la vida, y ya es algo que con la edad que tengo ya hay que empezar a mirar un poquito más. P. Cuénteme eso del corto aviso de UFC… R. Sí. Lo que pasa que una vez tenía ya pelea cerrada de atrás y la otra vez ni eché cuentas porque no venía por mi manager. Si yo estoy contento con mi mánager, ¿para qué le voy a estar echando cuentas a otros? P. Es bueno que ya se hable de usted para esas cosas. R. Sí, ya nos tienen en el radar. Vamos, ya hace tiempo, hace un par de años, me hicieron entrevistas para el The Ultimage Fighter (TUF). No me cogieron pero de todos modos le había dicho al manager que quería coger más experiencia, seguir formándome. O sea, ahora, si me ofrecieran un TUF… pues de cabeza, lo cojo, porque creo que ya estoy más que preparado y tengo el nivel más que de sobra. Y ya lo he podido contrastar en el Next Gen en cada entrenamiento. P. Me gusta que tenga tan claro que no hay que coger atajos para llegar a la meta… R. Yo, si hago las cosas, me gusta hacerlas bien. Yo no quiero llegar y ya está, yo quiero llegar y asentarme. Llegar y hacer dos peleas de contrato, tres peleas de contrato en UFC… ¿y luego qué?. ¿Me voy para mi casa y me siguen quedando siete, ocho años de carrera... con bolsas totalmente distintas? ¿Cómo va a ser la motivación mía para enfrentar esos combates? No como ahora, que si llego, va a ser un cambio en muchos aspectos grande… pero yo creo que ya tengo las bases o estoy construyendo las bases para poder decir... ‘Vale, es que puedo’. Entonces, bueno, si llego, puede que haga dos o tres peleas y me vaya para mi casa… pero ahora tenemos más recursos para poder asentarnos y hacer una carrera dentro de UFC. P. ¿Lo han intentado reclutar para pelear en España? WOW FC, por ejemplo… R. Sí, sí. Y me han tratado super bien. Yo tengo buena relación con Arturo, es un señor de los pies a la cabeza. Me invitaron a Sevilla, me dieron entradas para ir con mis compañeros… y estoy super agradecido con WOW. Y sí, me han llamado y eso, pero yo soy leal. Esta gente aquí en Inglaterra me está tratando de puta madre, mira lo que me están dando… Yo, de momento, además tengo contrato con ellos de exclusividad. Y hay que ser agradecidos en esta vida. Me están dando un lugar que yo ni me imaginaba y aparte, como siempre he dicho, ser campeón en Cage Warriors para mí es tema personal, de legado y todo. La gente que entiende de este deporte sabe que aquí se hacen las cosas muy bien, nadie regala nada. No digo que en España lo hagan, eh, pero construir legado en Cage Warriors es muy importante. Creo que a día de hoy todavía no es igual a construirlo en España. Por aquí han pasado Paddy, McGregor, Aspinall, Ilia peleó aquí, Hermansson, Della Maddalena, Herbert, Arnold Allena, Wood, Kavanagh.. es una locura. P. Usted debutó en profesional en 2023. Es decir, nueve peleas en tres años. ¿Ha tenido tiempo a pararse y reflexionar sobre lo que está logrando o va todo demasiado deprisa? R. Yo soy una persona muy agradecida. Entonces, a lo mejor no lo llego a asimilar, como que no me paro tanto a pensarlo… pero como que a veces cuando me paro y me siento yo, en plan, flipa. Quién me iba a decir esto cuando yo estaba en amateur. Es que, tío, estoy viviendo un sueño. No sé decirlo de otra manera, estoy viviendo un sueño. Y lo único que puedo decir es gracias. Y eso, estar agradecido de todo lo que he vivido, de todo lo que estoy viviendo, pero centrado en el momento actual que estoy en mi carrera y seguir avanzando, seguir avanzando para ver qué es lo que nos depara la vida. Estoy viviendo una vida que ni yo mismo me imaginaba que iba a acabar viviendo.

articles.title: 'What a fighter': Shikhar Dhawan celebrates Manisha Bhanwala's historic gold at Senior World Championships
articles.summary: From a six-point deficit to standing atop the world podium, Manisha Bhanwala scripted a historic chapter in Indian wrestling with a stunning comeback
articles.body: From a six-point deficit to standing atop the world podium, Manisha Bhanwala scripted a historic chapter in Indian wrestling with a stunning comeback victory in the women's 59kg final at the Senior World Championships in Astana, Kazakhstan. Her remarkable triumph drew congratulations from across the sporting fraternity, with former India cricketer Shikhar Dhawan leading the praise for the wrestler's fighting spirit.Manisha scripts history with stunning comeback in finalManisha produced an extraordinary turnaround against Nette on Friday, overturning a six-point deficit to secure an 8-6 victory and deliver India's maiden gold medal in the history of the Senior World Championships.The Indian wrestler endured a difficult start as Nette established a 5-0 advantage through a four-point throw and an additional point following India's unsuccessful challenge. A subsequent caution against Manisha extended the American's lead to 6-0, leaving the Indian with a mountain to climb.However, Manisha refused to surrender and opened her account with a stepout point before the break. She carried that momentum into the second period, executing a takedown to reduce the deficit.Another unsuccessful challenge from the American corner handed Manisha an additional point and an opportunity to attack from par terre. She capitalised with a two-point gut-wrench to level the scores at 6-6 before delivering the decisive pressure takedown to move ahead 8-6.Manisha then held her ground against Nette's attempts to regain the advantage, completing a memorable comeback to secure the gold medal.'What a fighter'Dhawan lauded Manisha for refusing to give up after falling 0-6 behind against the USA's Abigail Nette, eventually producing an 8-6 victory to become the first Indian to win a gold medal at the Senior World Championships.“From 0-6 down to becoming a World Champion! What a fighter, Manisha! You’ve made the entire nation proud. Congratulations!,” Dhawan wrote on X.Manisha's impressive run to the gold medalHer journey to the final was equally impressive. She began her campaign with a 6-2 victory over Canada's Laurence Beauregard in the pre-quarterfinals before overcoming Mongolia's Bolortuya Khurelkhuu in the semifinals to book her place in the gold-medal bout.Manisha's historic triumph also provided a major boost to India's campaign after the country endured disappointment in two other women's finals. Neelam in the 50kg category and Kajal in the 76kg category had to settle for silver medals.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'When down, Manisha sher ki tarah jhapatta maarti hai': How Bhanwala overturned 0-6 deficit to win historic gold at World Championships
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An athlete’s biggest test, perhaps, comes not when they’re dominating but when they’re down. When a match is going against them.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An athlete’s biggest test, perhaps, comes not when they’re dominating but when they’re down. When a match is going against them. When the clock is against them. When a glance at the scoreboard doesn’t give reason to breathe easy, Manisha Bhanwala, competing in the non-Olympic 59kg category, faced multiple challenges in the Wrestling World Championships final on Friday.At Astana’s Barys Arena, USA’s Abigail Nette led Bhanwala 6-0 in the first period and then 6-1 at the break. But a lapse from the American gave the 29-year-old Indian an ‘in’ which saw the deficit reduced to two points. With half a minute left, Bhanwala forced a takedown to take an 8-6 lead, which she held on to win a historic gold medal.How historic? Manisha Bhanwala had become the first Indian woman to win a gold medal at the Wrestling World Championships. She became the first Indian, male or female, to stand atop the podium since Sushil Kumar in 2010. At 29, she is the oldest of the 24 Indians to have won a medal at the World Championships.However, none of this would have been possible without the mental strength to overturn that 0-6 deficit.“Manisha and I sat and watched her (Nette) videos before the final. We observed that she gets tired in the fifth or sixth minute. After that, she would get exhausted. But, as a coach, as a guardian, there was a tiny bit of concern at 0-6,” said national coach Virender Kumar in a virtual interaction conducted by Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) from Astana on Saturday.“Still, I was confident that in these moments, Manisha starts to pounce like a lion. I knew she would take a lot of points in the fifth minute. She has the capability to take 10 points in a minute. In the 30-second break, I told Manisha that she would take a lot of points in the fifth or sixth minute. I was confident of it,” he continued.The seeds for such confidence and mental strength are sown in training. In sparring contests, she would experiment with different scenarios to keep herself ready for competitions: down 0-6, as was the case in the final, down 0-10 and other such virtual situations.Manisha took up wrestling late in her life, introduced to it by her late father Suresh, who she still fondly refers to as "Father Sahab".Born in Siwaha, 10 km outside Jind in Haryana, Manisha took up wrestling to please her father. As Manisha held the tricolour aloft and wore the gold medal around her neck, her father was with her.She wore a special t-shirt bearing his photograph during her warm-up. Prior to leaving for Kazakhstan, she got a white T-shirt printed and had the faces of her parents added to it."There is no 'idea' behind this. These things cannot be 'ideas'. These are feelings, something you just get from the inside. Three days before arriving in Astana, I got it done. I got it done because I had a feeling that I would come back with a medal, with a record," said Manisha.With brother Rinku a kabaddi player and sister-in-law Mamta Sihag a wrestler, the family knows a thing or two about heartbreak. None bigger than when Suresh passed away due to a cardiac arrest shortly before Manisha was set to leave for the 2022 Asian Championships in Mongolia.A distraught Manisha wished to skip the competition but her family reminded her of Suresh's dreams. Eventually, Manisha won a bronze medal there before adding three more Asian Championships medals, including a gold last year."My father has taught me one thing since childhood. If you get involved in any work, then finish it. That thing is in my blood. Don't get involved in any work if you don't plan on finishing it. For me, the first and last option is wrestling," said Manisha.My father has taught me one thing since childhood. If you get involved in any work, then finish it. That thing is in my bloodCoach Virender Kumar stressed her work ethic and dedication to the sport. "When I met Manisha for the first time in 2022, I was her junior coach. In the summers of May and June, the temperature was around 45 degrees. When she used to go for practise, she used to do it twice a day. At that time, I used to think, ‘Is this girl crazy?’”“Then, gradually, I got attached to her. This girl has no hobby, no interest in going out and watching movies, spend money on clothes, etc. She has only one hobby: wrestling. And the result of that is in front of you," he continued.Path to LA 2028 and shift to 57kg categoryThe big challenge for Manisha now is the shift to the 57kg category with the aim of not just qualifying for LA 2028 but winning a medal too. Having competed in multiple categories - 59kg, 57kg, 62kg, 65kg - Manisha's big challenge will be to maintain weight for the 57kg competition."When I won yesterday (Friday), the coach came in the evening. The whole team was there. The coach decided that training begins from the morning itself. Now we have the senior nationals and the PWL (Pro Wrestling League). When the India camp starts, we will start from there. The whole team will work on it. We will then reassess what to do, which competitions to play, and which not to play. The coach decides after speaking to the rest of the team," said Manisha.Coach Virender Kumar said Manisha can count on her wealth of experience when it comes to this highly competitive category."As a team member, there are more girls in 57kg. But after a year, the biggest thing will be the experience. If yesterday there was another girl in place of Manisha, who was trailing 0-6 in the final, I don't think she would have recovered from it."I will give an example. Look at Kajal, she is 18 years old. articles.summary: The king is back. But is he still the king?
articles.body:
The king is back. But is he still the king?

Pay-per-view stalwart Canelo Alvarez will walk from the locker room to the ring for the first time in 13 months on Saturday when he meets unbeaten WBC super middleweight champ Christian Mbilli at Kingdom Arena in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Alvarez last fought in September 2025 in Las Vegas, where he was schooled over 12 rounds by now-four-division elite Terence Crawford at Allegiant Stadium. Now 36, Alvarez has not won since he out-pointed William Scull over 12 rounds at ANB Arena in Riyadh in May 2025.

Prior to the Crawford fight, Alvarez had lost just twice—to Floyd Mayweather Jr. in 2013 and Dmitry Bivol in 2022. Both of those defeats also came in Las Vegas.

The Alvarez-Mbilli bout will headline a four-bout main card to be streamed by DAZN at 1 p.m. ET.

articles.summary: Canelo Alvarez returns to the boxing ring for the first time in over a year to challenge Christian Mbilli for the WBC super middleweight title.
articles.body:
Canelo Alvarez returns to the boxing ring for the first time in over a year to challenge Christian Mbilli for the WBC super middleweight title.

The last time we saw Alvarez in the ring he was on the wrong side of a unanimous decision loss to Terence Crawford. It was a career-defining performance for Bud, but the first time that Canelo has lost since May 2022.

Now, he's looking to reclaim the super middleweight title that has been with him for much of his career against a champion who is 31 and has an unbeaten record of 29-0-1.

Here's everything you need to know to catch the fight as well as a preview and prediction.

Fight Odds, Schedule and Scorecard Prediction

When: Saturday, October 31 at 1 p.m. ET (main event ringwalks at approximately 4:30 p.m.)

Where: Kingdom Arena, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Odds: Alvarez -290 ($290 bet to win $100); Mbilli +240 ($100 bet wins $240)

Prediction: Canelo wins via unanimous decision (116-112 x2, 118-110)

The biggest question surrounding this fight is whether Alvarez still has enough game to beat someone who will push the pace.

Mbillis' best attribute is his willingness to throw leather. He's an aggressive combination puncher who likes to push the pace.

Historically, those have been the kind of fighters who Canelo has flourished against. His tactical counter-punching has helped him neutralize fighters who are going to rush him in the past.

It's one of the reasons Alvarez said he wanted this fight.

"He's going to throw a lot of punches, I'm a counter-puncher," he told Matt Astbury of DAZN. "It's going to be a hard fight, but I enjoy that type of fight because at the end of the day, it's a lot of action, you can show a lot of things and you don't need to chase anything."

The question is whether Alvarez still has the reflexes and hand speed to counter. The superstar is now 36 with 21 years of professional fights under his belt. This will be the 69th time he makes the walk to the ring.

Mbilli is not an experienced world champion, but he is unbeaten in 30 professional fights with a belt to show for it.

However, Alvarez hasn't shown that much decline. He's not in his prime, but his loss to Crawford doesn't necessarily forecast a loss to someone on Mbilli's level.

This should be another demonstration of Alvarez's skill on the way to another win.

articles.title: UFC champion Islam Makhachev says his next fight will be ‘one of last’
articles.summary: Makhachev, one of the best fighters in UFC history, wants to face the winner of next year’s Prates vs Morales fight.
articles.body:
Reigning UFC welterweight champion Islam Makhachev has hinted at an imminent retirement, saying his next fight will be “one of the last” of his mixed martial arts career.

“My next fight is one of the last in my career,” the Russian MMA fighter said on X on Friday night.

The Russian-born Dagestani fighter has expressed a desire to face the winner of the upcoming bout between Carlos Prates and Michael Morales in a bid to prove to the world “who is the best”.

Makhachev (29 wins, one loss) successfully defended his UFC welterweight championship belt in August, defeating ‌‌Ireland’s Ian Machado Garry via unanimous decision in the main event of UFC 330 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.

With that, Makhachev etched his ⁠⁠name in the UFC record books, extending his winning streak to 17 consecutive fights and surpassing UFC Hall of Famer Anderson Silva’s historic 16-fight mark set from 2006 to 2013.

Makhachev, the UFC’s pound-for-pound top-ranked fighter, now wants to test himself against the winner of the UFC fight between Prates and Morales, the interim welterweight title fight scheduled for January 30, 2027, the co-main event of UFC 336 in Toronto, Canada.

“They say Prates is too dangerous for me and Morales is too good for me. So I want to face the best of them and prove to the world once again who is the best in the world,” he added.

UFC CEO Dana White said earlier this month that Makhachev was originally slated to defend his welterweight title against Prates in January, but the 35-year-old instead opted to wait for the winner of an interim title bout between Prates and Morales.

Makhachev, widely regarded as one of the best fighters in UFC history, will observe the Muslim holy month of Ramadan in February and early March in 2027 before returning in the second quarter of the year.

“On average, Islam fights like once a year,” White said at a media conference.

“He was slated for January, and then said, ‘I don’t want to fight until after Ramadan.’ You can’t hold up divisions like this. You gotta keep moving.

“This fight [between Prates and Morales] makes sense.”

Speaking to Russian outlet pound4padel, former lightweight champion Makhachev said the Prates-Morales fight will decide “the true, worthy contender”.

articles.standfirst: Lorenzo Mattia Berlusconi, de 16 años, persigue el sueño de ser olímpico
articles.summary: Lorenzo Mattia Berlusconi, de 16 años, persigue el sueño de ser olímpico
articles.body: Lorenzo Mattia Berlusconi tiene 16 años. No le pesa el apellido. Es nieto de Silvio Berlusconi, el que fuera presidente del Milan, magnate de los medios de comunicación y primer ministro de Italia. Hace una semana sumó su cuarta victoria en otros tantos combates organizados por la Federación Italiana de Boxeo. En total lleva 10 triunfos si se suman los cosechados en el circuito Kombat Tour Italia. La pasión por el boxeo la lleva en los genes. Su padre, Pier Silvio, director general de Mediaset, practicó karate y boxeo cuando era joven. Su hijo Lorenzo, antes de elegir el deporte del cuadrilátero, también se enfundó el karategui. Comenzó a entrenarse con Amedeo Marai, entrenador del gimnasio Area Bastarda de Rapallo. Allí, al principio nadie conocía quien era su familia para, según su entrenador, "protegerlo y permitirle integrarse en el grupo sin que su apellido se convirtiera en un elemento distintivo". Su primer combate lo disputó el 13 de diciembre de 2025 en Savona. Desde entonces, cada vez que se ha enfudado los guantes ha salido victoriosos. Lorenzo, que compite para el equipo Clan Area, subió al ring en la categoría sub 17 (-60 kg) y venció por puntos a Oscar Acciai, del Ardita Boxing Club, para sumar su décimo triunfo tras un combate a tres asaltos. Su carrera en el boxeo amateur acaba de arrancar, pero ya tiene como objetivo poder representar a Italia en unos Juegos Olímpicos.
